text.p: Aides to House Speaker Newt Gingrich on Thursday dismissed as "absurd" allegations that a former campaign volunteer engaged in improper political activity during Gingrich's re-election to Congress in 1990.
The former volunteer, Steve Lane, told Reuters he had spoken to the FBI and local police about a stolen cache of documents and tapes which he said would corroborate his allegations.
"I consider the allegations made by Steve Lane to be utterly absurd," Nancy Desmond, Gingrich's district director, said in a statement.

"Any time we receive any allegation that implies legal wrongdoing, it is our policy to turn it over to the appropriate law enforcement authority. Concerning Steve Lane, I have contacted the local FBI office and presented them with the relevant information," she added.
The Los Angeles Times on Thursday quoted Gingrich aides as saying Lane demanded money in exchange for keeping quiet about alleged activities including political espionage during the 1990 campaign.
As a result, the newspaper reported, Gingrich's office in Marietta, Georgia, filed an extortion complaint with the FBI against him on Monday for attempted blackmail.
The FBI declined to comment but a Gingrich spokesman said the FBI was investigating.

Lane told Reuters he met longtime Gingrich advisor and biographer Mel Steely on Dec. 30 and offered to keep quiet about his claims in exchange for recognition from the speaker and help for local environmental groups. But he denied he was asking for money.
Hours later, he said, someone broke into a mobile home he uses as an office and stole boxes of documents and tapes dealing with his alleged campaign activities.

A Gingrich press aide in Washington protested to the Los Angeles Times in a letter dated Wednesday, saying the newspaper would be guilty of "irresponsible journalism" for publishing Lane's allegations.

A 46-year-old self-employed consultant, Lane said his dispute with the Gingrich staff dated back to a tough 1990 Congressional race which the Georgia Republican nearly lost to Democrat David Worley. Gingrich spent nearly $1.5 million in the campaign and was re-elected by a margin of only 974 votes.
As part of that campaign, Lane said Gingrich staff members instructed him to spy on Democrats and environmental groups.
He said he discussed the allegations with FBI agents for seven hours at his home last week, after the documents and tapes were stolen.

"I have written down 25 allegations (against the Gingrich campaign), which the authorities who came out here and looked at the information I have, put in four categories -- just politics, unethical behaviour, potential state laws that were broken and potential federal laws that were broken," Lane said in a telephone interview.

"I'm somewhat limited ... to talking about anything that fell into first to categories." He said the theft that followed his meeting with Steely was of little mportance because "I have duplicates of everything."
"I never made any demands whatsoever upon Mel Steely. Never discussed money with him," Lane said.

"These allegations are totally trumped up to punish me for speaking out in the past and to silence me from any future comments I may make that may jeopardise Congressman Gingrich's political future or Mel's book deal."
The allegations surfaced just days after Gingrich was narrowly re-elected as speaker of the House of Representatives.
